title: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'
description: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington
body: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFederal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat. Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump.A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child. Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.Homeland Security Investigations Police remove documents from the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) on Oct. 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Leyden | Getty Images"I'm ok," Omar wrote. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote."I will not be silenced."Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.""This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said.Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.""For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States."There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid."The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the Democratic Caucus chair, in a statement."For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," the statement said. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.""The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice."

schema.headline: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'

title: Meta debuts Muse Wonder AI model in latest test of users' willingness to pay
description: watch nowMeta debuted its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. B
body: watch nowMeta debuted its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. But it doesn't come for free. To access the model, users of the Muse personal agent app will need to sign up for a monthly subscription of $20 or $100. The release underscores Meta's efforts to create new AI-derived revenue sources outside of its core online ad business.   Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Monday that the company developed Muse Wonder, codenamed Watermelon, to improve the capabilities of "personal and professional agents" so they don't stumble on tasks like booking dinner reservations and checking for availabilities."When you do real-world tasks, you're going to get roadblocks and you're going to get things that come up or various setbacks,"  Wang said. "We specifically tried to train the model to be able to try other approaches instead of stalling and then checking back in with the user at any time."Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive officer of Meta Platforms Inc., reveals the Muse Charm device during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMeta said in a blog post that the latest model "offers our strongest safeguards to date" against "cyber misuse." Those protections only come with the paid model for now.Muse shot up to the top of Apple's App Store after Meta introduced the AI agent app last month. The app is free, with subscription plans available for more usage. Wang said Meta's AI team has been monitoring for agent-related "incidents or issues" with Muse in order to understand problems and resolve them. Some users have complained on social media that the agent accessed personal messages without authorization, which the company has disputed.    Meta is trying to better inform people of how to use the app to avoid certain problems, Wang said. "I think there are certainly instances users have authorized various communications or whatnot earlier in a conversation, and then may have forgotten about that," Wang said. He added that the company is educating users on such matters "to ensure that consumers can trust the product going forward."Muse Wonder will also be available to coders who pay to access the company's related Meta Model API. Wang said that offering will cost more than the standard subscriptions because it is a "much larger model and at frontier level." He said it will still be priced "meaningfully below" leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic.An even more powerful variant of Meta's latest model, dubbed Muse Wonder Full, will only be available to developers who sign up to the company's software engineering focused Muse Code AI agent under a $50 or $200 a month subscription plan.WATCH: Meta partners with companies to set standards for doing business with AI bots.watch now

schema.headline: Meta debuts Muse Wonder AI model in latest test of users' willingness to pay

title: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn on October 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. Aaro
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn on October 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. Aaron Schwartz | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism.Trump, in a Truth Social post, accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union."The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote. While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months. The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin, ends the war against Ukraine."The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal."While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent, however.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

schema.headline: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'

title: Parenting in the digital age can be ‘a very anxiety provoking experience,’ says Emily Oster: How parents can lower that anxiety
description: If all parents read were the headlines, they'd know two things about AI: "There's a 10% chance that it's going to kill us all." And, they'd know "it's
body: If all parents read were the headlines, they'd know two things about AI: "There's a 10% chance that it's going to kill us all." And, they'd know "it's, like, incredibly dangerous for teens." That's according to Emily Oster, parenting expert and economics professor at Brown University who sat down with CNBC Make It at OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens Parent Forum on Wednesday.As she noted, today's parents (along with everyone else) have to navigate a regular onslaught of doomsday coverage about the dangers of new and existing tech. "That is a very anxiety provoking experience" for a parent, says Oster.Even so, before you try to restrict your kids to their bedroom until they're 18 — or set any other boundaries as a result of that fear and paranoia, here's what Oster recommends.Equip yourselfWhen new online platforms start proliferating and the internet weighs in, the first thing you can do is get informed, suggests Oster. "I do think there is value for parents in exploring some of these tools," she adds. The goal does not have to be to make any decision about how your child should use them. It's just about getting a first-hand understanding of what these platforms are.You might discover they're not as scary as they seem. Or even if you remain concerned, you'll have a better understanding of what those boundaries should be. "You're coming into the conversation feeling more empowered," she says. Control your domainWith kids, the best way to avoid falling victim to the doom and gloom is to take control of the spaces where you have greater influence: Your home. "A stable home environment with parents who love them, who are supporting them," says Oster, "that is the thing that you control." She adds that "we probably spend too little time investing in this thing that we control relative to worrying about what's happening outside."Research supports the idea of the key role a home life plays in a child's upbringing. One that is warm, open and includes appropriate limits is associated with higher self-esteem and better school performance, among other outcomes, according to the American Psychological Association.At your house, focus on that love and support as well as the parameters you can set, such as no screens or phones overnight. And when you need encouragement, remember "how important that foundation is for when you send your kid out into the world," says Oster.

schema.headline: Parenting in the digital age can be ‘a very anxiety provoking experience,’ says Emily Oster: How parents can lower that anxiety

title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck
description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026. Tsai Hsin-han | ReutersSINGAPORE — The chief executives o
body: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026. Tsai Hsin-han | ReutersSINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models."[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns."If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said.Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.Read more CNBC tech newsAI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlightMicrosoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans controlNvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing themHollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AIHock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands."[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now."He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online.Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure."There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030.Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power.But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said.Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau.Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.watch now

schema.headline: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck

title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
description: A Microsoft Azure Maia 300 prototype chip.MicrosoftMicrosoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance o
body: A Microsoft Azure Maia 300 prototype chip.MicrosoftMicrosoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack. Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, Cerebras, Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD. Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline."We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.Read more CNBC tech newsAI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlightMicrosoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans controlNvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing themHollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AIMicrosoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs."We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have,"  Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well."Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies."Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI tradewatch now

schema.headline: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia

title: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack
description: Beth Hammack, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, during a research conference at the Federal Reserve Bank
body: Beth Hammack, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, during a research conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas in Dallas, Texas, US, on Friday, Oct. 31, 2025. Desiree Rios | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesCleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Monday that tighter monetary policy might be needed to bring down inflation and the central bank should make fast, incremental adjustments."When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," Hammack, a voting member of the Fed's policymaking committee, said in prepared remarks delivered during the National Association of Business Economics annual gathering."Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation," Hammack added.Hammack's comments signal that more interest rate hikes could be on the horizon. Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come.The Fed last month voted to increase interest rates for the first time in three years.Traders priced in a more than 78% likelihood that the central bank keeps rates unchanged at its policy meeting later this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool. But they see a nearly 88% chance of a hike at the Fed's final meeting of the year in December.Sticky inflation poses challenges for consumers, businesses and monetary policymakers alike, Hammack said. The Cleveland Fed chief said that, with the "breadth" of current inflationary pressures, she expects it will take "some time" to get annual price growth down to the central bank's goal of 2%.The personal consumption expenditures price index came in at 3.4% year over year in August. The so-called core reading of the index, which strips out volatile food and energy costs and is favored by the Fed, registered at 3% compared with a year prior."Long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years," Hammack said. "But I'm not taking that for granted.""With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," she said.

schema.headline: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack

title: Inflation likely peaked for 2026 but will remain sticky, according to prediction markets
description: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesTraders on prediction market platform Kalshi think
body: Customers shop at a grocery store on Sept. 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesTraders on prediction market platform Kalshi think inflation likely reached a peak for the year, though they don't see a sharp move lower anytime soon. Traders think the September consumer price index, due Wednesday at 8:30 a.m. ET, will show a 3.6% increase year over year. That's in line with a FactSet consensus estimate. That would mark an increase from the 3.4% advance seen in August. Yet speculators on Kalshi place just under one-in-three odds that inflation will hit new highs in 2026. Previously, year-over-year inflation peaked at 4.2% in May.Inflation-related contracts on the platform ask traders if they think that CPI will come in above various levels for the month of September or if it will go above certain levels at any point in 2026. The contracts are resolved using the official data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Core inflation is predicted to remain steady at 2.4% year over year, also in line with economists' estimates, according to FactSet. However, traders think that core inflation — which excludes food and energy price changes — will remain elevated throughout the rest of 2026.There's just a 6% chance that core inflation falls below 2.2% this year. Annual core inflation was last below that level before the spike in inflation that began in 2021.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Inflation likely peaked for 2026 but will remain sticky, according to prediction markets

title: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
description: Secretary General of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Ellen Moons (C), Chair of the Prize Committee John Hassler (L) and Member of the Prize Comm
body: Secretary General of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences Ellen Moons (C), Chair of the Prize Committee John Hassler (L) and Member of the Prize Committee and expert Timo Boppart announce U.S. economists Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford as the winners of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on October 12, 2026.Jonathan Nackstrand | Afp | Getty ImagesRobert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were on Monday awarded the Nobel memorial prize in economics for work that underpins the models used by central banks and governments to "smooth out" periods of boom and bust.The U.S.-born pair were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" that contribute to macroeconomic stability. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was established by Sweden's central bank in 1968. The winners will split a 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) prize. Hall, born in California, is a professor at Stanford University, while Massachusetts-born Woodford is a professor at Columbia University. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. Rethinking economic modelsDuring the stagflationary oil crises of the 1970s, widely accepted Keynesian models — which prescribed cutting interest rates and increasing government budget deficits to tackle recessions — seemed to "no longer work," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.To revitalize these models, the economists' separate work has looked beyond macroeconomic variables such as inflation, production and consumption and showed how individual households and businesses collectively shape the economy through decision-making based on their expectations for the future, the academy said. Their work has shown the importance of central banks and governments communicating their policy plans, which can "influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction," it said."On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy added."Since the new models' introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us."The economics memorial prize is the last to be announced, following the original Nobel Prizes in physiology or medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.This year's laureates include Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work promoting peace and international law, and Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, who won the literature prize for a "bold and inventive oeuvre."

schema.headline: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford

title: Trump Media advisor Katie Zacharia named White House press secretary
description: Katie Zacharia attends the Nashville premiere of 'David' at AMC DINE-IN Thoroughbred 20 on December 14, 2025 in Franklin, Tennessee.Terry Wyatt | Gett
body: Katie Zacharia attends the Nashville premiere of 'David' at AMC DINE-IN Thoroughbred 20 on December 14, 2025 in Franklin, Tennessee.Terry Wyatt | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Sunday named Katie Zacharia, a lawyer and conservative commentator at Trump Media & Technology, to be the next White House press secretary."I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the Press Briefing Room in the White House," the president wrote in a Truth Social post. "Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!" he added.Zacharia, a self-described "hardline Trump supporter," succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Leavitt went on maternity leave after giving birth to her second child earlier this year. She is expected to join Fox News as an on-air contributor next month.According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has worked since June as a senior communications advisor for Trump Media, which owns the president's preferred social media outlet, Truth Social.Her profile also shows that she serves as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative activist group founded by Richard Grenell, Trump's special presidential envoy for special missions and former head of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.In March, Zacharia finished a two-month stint as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, according to her LinkedIn page.Zacharia's IMDb page lists dozens of appearances on Fox News political talk shows and other conservative outlets.— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Trump Media advisor Katie Zacharia named White House press secretary

title: McDonald's is leaning into chicken and drinks to grow. New data shows it could be a tough task
description: A chicken sandwich from McDonald's is shown in Chicago, Illinois, May 6, 2021.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesMcDonald's is betting on chicken and beverages
body: A chicken sandwich from McDonald's is shown in Chicago, Illinois, May 6, 2021.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesMcDonald's is betting on chicken and beverages to fuel its next phase of growth, but new consumer spending data suggests the fast-food giant faces stiff competition from rivals that specialize in those areas.At its September investor day, McDonald's outlined plans to gain an additional 1.5 percentage points of global market share in both chicken and beverages by 2030. The chain identified the categories as significant opportunities to expand its business beyond beef. CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC the size of those markets underscores the potential upside."Chicken is a $130 billion category. We have about a 20% share of chicken. Beverages is about a $230 billion category. We have a 10% share of beverages," Kempczinski said, saying McDonald's has more room to grow in those areas than in the $50 billion global beef category, where it has about a 40% share.But new data indicates McDonald's could have a tough task in gaining spending from chicken and drink rivals. Many of the restaurant chains winning the most spending from McDonald's diners specialize in those two segments, according to exclusive data shared by Consumer Edge, which tracks credit and debit card transactions.Among McDonald's customers, Chick-fil-A gained 0.58 percentage points of limited-service restaurant spending in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, making it the biggest gainer among the chains tracked by Consumer Edge.Coffee businesses are also capturing more spending from McDonald's customers. Drive-thru-only chain 7 Brew added 0.4 percentage points, while Starbucks, Dutch Bros. Coffee and Dunkin' also ranked among the top 10 gainers. Together, the four coffee chains added 0.88 percentage points of spending share. McDonald's remained by far the largest individual chain in customers' overall limited-service restaurant spending, but its share declined from a year earlier. Restaurant Brands International-owned Burger King, meanwhile, gained 0.24 percentage points, the largest increase among burger chains. "There’s a big battle for a smaller amount of restaurant spend as people become more selective in what they spend," said Michael Gunther, Consumer Edge senior vice president.The data says only so much about the competitive landscape for McDonald's in the chicken and drink spaces, in part because they don't track exactly what customers are ordering at the counter."If they [McDonald's] are able to attract diners with interesting options, it could work,” Gunther added.While McDonald's has struggled with sluggish sales, executives have said they saw signs of improvement toward the end of the third quarter. At its investor day, McDonald's said U.S. comparable sales were slightly negative in July and August, but the company said it expected September to turn positive. Consumer Edge data similarly showed McDonald's year-over-year spending share declines narrowing across every income group in September. Wall Street has also questioned how quickly the chicken and beverage strategy can deliver. Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo said after McDonald's investor day that U.S. beverage launches had not generated enough sales to offset broader weakness, while the company's next chicken platform — which includes hand-breaded chicken and grilled chicken menu items — was further away than he expected."The scale of investment required to deliver [the company's growth plan] McDonald's Next was above our expectations and introduces additional pressure on near-term earnings," said Gargiulo in his note.He has a market perform rating on the stock and $295 price target. Shares closed around $235 on Friday.

schema.headline: McDonald's is leaning into chicken and drinks to grow. New data shows it could be a tough task

title: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
description: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October
body: Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.Saudi Ministry of Media | ReutersThe Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital.King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after strikes that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300. Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week.Air traffic in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12, 2026.Courtesy: Flightradar24The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region.The FAA late Sunday said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10.Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia, but the country's flights and passenger counts had climbed in recent years. The route between Riyadh to Jeddah in the country's west was the fifth-busiest in the world last year, according to aviation-data firm OAG.Delta Air Lines had been scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23 but the carrier on Monday said it would delay that service until March.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

schema.headline: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks

title: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads
description: US President Donald Trump speaks during a Columbus Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2026. Alex Wro
body: US President Donald Trump speaks during a Columbus Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on October 9, 2026. Alex Wroblewski | Afp | Getty ImagesA federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics call political propaganda intended to influence the November midterm election.The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million allocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads.The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon the ads would not continue airing past Sunday. Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired.The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.Congress appropriated the money for the ads for immigration enforcement.The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block the ads told Rochon earlier Sunday that she should issue the TRO despite the U.S. Attorney's Office's claim that the ads would not continue past Sunday."Defendants admit that appropriated funds were used to pay for political ads and do not disputethat this use of taxpayer money is unlawful," the plaintiffs said in a court filing Sunday. "Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. "Indeed, Defendants assert — boldly, given their failure to defend the ads on the merits — that ads will continue to air today, including during evening programming that will attract millions of viewers."Rochon agreed, saying in her order that the U.S. Attorney's statement that the ads would stop Sunday did not render the TRO request moot. The judge also rejected the Justice Department's argument that the coalition lacked legal standing to challenge the ads.Rochon said the coalition has shown it is likely to win the lawsuit, would suffer irreparable harm if the TRO is not granted, and that "an injunction serves the public interest."In addition, the judge ordered the Trump administration not to enter into any new agreements or expand existing ones for the ads. And she stayed a purchase order for the ads between U.S. Customs and Border Protection and a contractor, Lepugh Inc., doing business as LMD Agency Inc.Rochon said she would soon issue a full opinion explaining her ruling.The coalition, which filed its lawsuit on Oct. 7, includes the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City.The Democratic National Committee filed a separate lawsuit challenging the ads that same day. The ads, which have aired for weeks, drew criticism from Democrats who said they seem designed to help Trump's fellow Republicans in November's election, which will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress.In its lawsuit, the coalition described one ad, titled "The Country He Loves," as featuring "rapid cuts of photos and videos of President Trump mixed in with text touting what the President views as his accomplishments in office," which includes "Largest Tax Cuts in History;" "Reigniting American Manufacturing;" and "Defend Law and Order and Police.""Between those messages, the screen repeatedly flashes the words "AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY," the civil complaint noted.Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Sept. 24, a day after that ad first aired."The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,'" Hassan wrote.Trump, in response to that criticism, said on Oct. 5 that, going forward, he or his super PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads. The White House later said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the ads that had already aired.In a statement Sunday evening on Rochon's order, the coalition said, "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.""There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the coalition said, referring to Trump."As this case moves forward and voters make their voices heard in this election, we will work to ensure the rule of law continues to be upheld, protecting the rights of voters and our democracy."

schema.headline: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads

title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
description: Vice President JD Vance speaks alongside, from left to right, White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller, U.S. Att
body: Vice President JD Vance speaks alongside, from left to right, White House Deputy Chief of Staff and Homeland Security Advisor Stephen Miller, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson during a press conference regarding a federal investigation alleging fraud and abuse of the H-1B visa program, in Washington, Oct. 8, 2026.Alex Wroblewski | AFP | Getty ImagesAs the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft, claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.Who's on the listAll eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45.The biggest sponsor wasn't suspendedAmazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. ... Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them.JD VanceVice President of the United StatesWhat the numbers showThe numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

schema.headline: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows

title: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
description: watch nowStarbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover."Starbuck
body: watch nowStarbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover."Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer. Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies. On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025, when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports. Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

schema.headline: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
